course.title: Databases and Data Modelling
course.description: Model data as tables and keys, remove redundancy without losing information, make queries fast with indexes, keep data correct under failure and concurrency, and learn when key-value and document stores fit.
course.audience: Someone who can already write SQL queries with joins, grouping and window functions (SQL: From Rows to Reports) and now wants to design the tables behind them and understand how a database behaves under load and failure. PostgreSQL is the reference system; examples are checked in SQLite where noted.

paragraphs: A relational database stores facts in tables and promises that what it stores stays true while programs read it and change it. Whether the promise holds is settled by decisions made long before any query is written. If a customer's email address is kept in three places, one of them will eventually be changed and the others will not, and no SELECT can say which copy is right. If the column a query filters on has no index, the database has to read the whole table to answer it. If two transfers of money touch the same account at once, or the machine stops between the two halves of one, the balances can end at figures that no sequence of whole transfers would produce.

Each of these decisions can be checked by hand. Asking which column of a wide table determines which others shows where a fact is repeated, and rejoining the pieces of a split table and counting the rows shows whether anything was lost. An index is a tree of pages, so the number of pages a lookup reads follows from the number of rows and the number of entries a page can hold, and writing out the order in which the steps of two transactions interleave shows what each of them can see. The same habit of counting and tracing also lets you say what a key-value store or a document store gives up in return for its speed and its simple layout, and why a relational database is usually the first one to try.
outcomes: You'll be able to turn a description of a business into entities, keys and relationships.
You'll be able to normalise a wide table to third normal form and check the decomposition loses nothing.
You'll be able to explain why an index speeds a lookup and which queries it serves.
You'll be able to read a query plan and compare join strategies.
You'll be able to predict the outcome of a failure in the middle of a transaction and name concurrency anomalies.
You'll be able to say what key-value and document stores trade away, and choose a store for a workload.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on SQL: From Rows to Reports.

modules.title: Modelling and normalisation
modules.description: Turn a described situation into tables, keys and constraints, then remove redundancy that causes errors.

modules.title: Indexes and query plans
modules.description: Why an index makes a lookup fast, which queries it serves, and how to read what the database plans to do.

modules.title: Transactions and isolation
modules.description: Keep data correct when statements fail halfway and when many users act at once.

modules.title: Beyond one relational database
modules.description: Key-value stores, documents, replication and sharding, and how to choose.

concepts.title: Entity
concepts.summary: An entity is a kind of thing the system must remember and tell apart, such as a patient or an appointment, and it becomes a table.

concepts.title: Attribute
concepts.summary: An attribute is a fact about one entity, stored as a column, and a fact about two entities together belongs to the relationship.

concepts.title: Cardinality
concepts.summary: Cardinality states how many of one entity may relate to one of another: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

concepts.title: Foreign key
concepts.summary: A foreign key is a column whose values must match a key in another table, which records a relationship and lets the database check it.

concepts.title: Junction table
concepts.summary: A many-to-many relationship is stored as a table of pairs, one row per pair, whose key is the combination of the two foreign keys.

concepts.title: Attributes of a relationship
concepts.summary: A fact that belongs to the pair rather than to either side, such as a grade, is a column of the junction table.

concepts.title: Primary key
concepts.summary: A primary key is a column or set of columns that is unique and non-null for every row and identifies it.

concepts.title: Natural and surrogate keys
concepts.summary: A natural key comes from the data, such as an ISBN, while a surrogate key is a meaningless identifier the database generates.

concepts.title: Constraint
concepts.summary: A constraint (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY) makes the database refuse data that breaks a rule, whichever application sends it.

concepts.title: Anomaly
concepts.summary: An anomaly is a data error that the structure of a table invites, such as changing a fact in one row and leaving it unchanged in another.

concepts.title: Functional dependency
concepts.summary: A functional dependency X -> Y holds when any two rows with the same X always have the same Y.

concepts.title: Candidate key
concepts.summary: A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that functionally determines every other column.

concepts.title: Normal forms
concepts.summary: 1NF requires atomic values, 2NF removes dependencies on part of a key, 3NF removes dependencies of non-key columns on other non-key columns, and BCNF requires every determinant to be a key.

concepts.title: Decomposition
concepts.summary: Normalising splits a table along its dependencies so that each fact is stored once.

concepts.title: Lossless join
concepts.summary: A decomposition is lossless when joining the parts returns exactly the original rows, which is guaranteed when the shared columns are a key of one part.

concepts.title: Fact table
concepts.summary: A fact table records events with numeric measures and foreign keys to dimensions, one row per event.

concepts.title: Dimension table
concepts.summary: A dimension table describes the who, what and when of facts, and is wide and small compared with the fact table.

concepts.title: Denormalisation
concepts.summary: Denormalising copies data to avoid joins at read time, trading write simplicity and consistency for read speed.

concepts.title: Page
concepts.summary: A database stores rows in fixed-size pages and reads and writes whole pages, so cost is counted in pages.

concepts.title: B-tree index
concepts.summary: A B-tree keeps keys sorted in pages with many children each, so its height grows with the logarithm of the row count in base fan-out.

concepts.title: Lookup cost
concepts.summary: A lookup reads one page per tree level plus the table page holding the row, instead of every table page.

concepts.title: Leftmost prefix
concepts.summary: An index on (a, b) is sorted by a and then by b within each a, so it can seek on a, or on a and b, but not on b alone.

concepts.title: Selectivity
concepts.summary: Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition keeps, and an index pays off when that fraction is small.

concepts.title: Covering index
concepts.summary: When an index holds every column a query reads, the database answers from the index without visiting the table.

concepts.title: Query plan
concepts.summary: A plan is the tree of steps the planner chose, with an estimated cost and row count at each step.

concepts.title: Join strategies
concepts.summary: A nested-loop join checks every pair unless the inner side has an index, a hash join builds a hash table on one side and probes it with the other, and a merge join walks two sorted inputs.

concepts.title: Planner statistics
concepts.summary: The planner uses stored statistics to estimate rows, and a large gap between estimated and actual rows usually means statistics are stale or missing.

concepts.title: Transaction
concepts.summary: A transaction groups statements so that they take effect together or not at all.

concepts.title: Atomicity
concepts.summary: Atomicity means that if a transaction does not commit, none of its changes are visible after recovery.

concepts.title: Durability and the log
concepts.summary: Durability means that once commit returns, a crash will not lose the change, which databases ensure by writing a commit record to a log on stable storage before acknowledging.

concepts.title: Concurrency anomalies
concepts.summary: Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update and write skew are named patterns of interleaving that produce results no serial order would.

concepts.title: Isolation level
concepts.summary: An isolation level states which anomalies the database promises to prevent: in PostgreSQL, Read Committed (the default), Repeatable Read and Serializable.

concepts.title: Write skew
concepts.summary: Write skew occurs when two transactions read overlapping data, each updates a different row, and together they break a rule neither broke alone; snapshot isolation allows it and serializable prevents it.

concepts.title: Multiversion concurrency control
concepts.summary: MVCC keeps old versions of a row so that readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create new versions, so readers do not block writers.

concepts.title: Row lock and deadlock
concepts.summary: Writers lock the rows they change, and two transactions that each wait for a lock the other holds are in a deadlock that the database resolves by aborting one.

concepts.title: Optimistic version check
concepts.summary: An update that includes the expected version in its WHERE clause changes zero rows if someone else got there first.

concepts.title: Key-value store
concepts.summary: A key-value store maps a key to a value and offers fast get, set and delete by key; it does not search by value.

concepts.title: Document model
concepts.summary: A document store keeps a nested record, usually JSON, under a key and can query its fields, so data read together can be stored together.

concepts.title: Access-pattern design
concepts.summary: In these stores the schema follows the queries that must be fast, rather than the entities alone.

concepts.title: Replication
concepts.summary: Replication keeps copies of data on several nodes for availability and read capacity, and asynchronous copies lag behind the primary.

concepts.title: Quorum
concepts.summary: With N replicas, writes acknowledged by W and reads from R, every read overlaps the latest write when R + W > N.

concepts.title: Sharding
concepts.summary: Sharding splits keys across nodes; hashing by key mod the node count is simple but moves most keys when the count changes, which consistent hashing avoids.

lessons.title: From a story to entities

steps.headline: An entity is a kind of thing the system must remember and tell apart, and each entity becomes a table.

lead.text: Take the clinic sentence one clause at a time. "4 doctors" names something the clinic has to be able to point at individually, so that this doctor can be told from that one, and it names something about which the clinic keeps facts, such as a name and a licence number. A kind of thing that can be told apart one by one and that has facts of its own is called an **entity**, and in a relational database each entity becomes a table whose rows are the individual things.

Patients pass the same test. So do appointments, which may be surprising because an appointment is an event rather than a person; the clinic still has to tell one from another, and it records a time against each. A phone number is different: nobody asks to identify a phone number apart from the patient who owns it, so it gives a fact about a patient and is not a kind of thing in its own right.

afterFigure.text: The test depends on what the system is for. A telephone company must identify individual numbers and record facts about each, so for it a phone number *is* an entity. The clinic is not that company, which is why you decide from the questions the system has to answer and not from the grammar of the sentence.

reveal.text: Seven clauses gave three entities. The rest of the lesson places the other facts and connects the three.

steps.headline: An attribute is one fact about one entity, stored as a column, and each fact belongs with the entity it describes.

lead.text: A fact stored about an entity is called an **attribute**, and it becomes a column of that entity's table. The start time and the room number describe an appointment, and the phone number describes a patient. The question to ask of any fact is *what is this a fact about?*, and the answer names the table that should hold it.

The date of an appointment shows why the question matters. It is tempting to write the date beside the patient, since patients are who the clinic thinks about first, but a patient with three appointments has three dates, and one column in the patient row has room for only one. The date changes from appointment to appointment, so it is a fact about the appointment.

afterFigure.text: A fact about *two* entities together, such as which doctor a patient saw, is not an attribute of either. It belongs to the relationship between them, which the next screens describe.

reveal.text: The same question places the room number and the phone number: each goes with the entity it describes.
The answer fixes whether the connection is one-to-many or many-to-many, which decides how the tables are built.

steps.headline: Cardinality states how many of one entity can relate to one of another, and it has to be asked in both directions.

lead.text: The number of things on each end of a relationship is its **cardinality**. Between two entities A and B there are three possible answers: **one-to-one**, when each A relates to at most one B and each B to at most one A; **one-to-many**, when each A may relate to many Bs but each B relates to only one A; and **many-to-many**, when both sides may have several. Each question is asked of one side at a time, and a statement is complete only when the question has been asked from both.

In the clinic a patient may see several doctors, and a doctor sees many patients, so the direct link between them is many-to-many. A single column cannot hold that, because neither table could name one partner. The clinic already has the thing that sits between them, which is the appointment: it belongs to exactly one patient and exactly one doctor, so the many-to-many link is replaced by two one-to-many links, and the appointment is the 'many' end of both.

afterFigure.text: If the table linked each patient to each doctor at most once, 4 doctors and 30 patients would allow up to 4 × 30 = 120 rows. Appointments can outnumber that, since the same pair can meet again on another date, which is why the appointment is a kind of thing with a date of its own and not just a pair.

steps.headline: An entity-relationship diagram can be checked by reading each line aloud as two sentences, one in each direction.

lead.text: Peter Chen proposed drawing models as entities and relationships in 1976, six years after E. F. Codd's paper had introduced the relational model of tables. His diagrams are still read in the same way: a line between two boxes says something in both directions. For the clinic, "a patient has many appointments" is one sentence and "an appointment belongs to exactly one patient" is its partner, and the pair together gives the cardinality of that line.

If either sentence sounds wrong when you say it, the model is wrong, and it is far cheaper to find that out on paper than after the tables hold data. The same reading catches a missing entity: when a sentence needs a word like "which" or "on" to be complete, as in "a patient sees a doctor *on* a date", there is a fact that belongs to neither entity alone.

steps.headline: Decide whether room should be an entity or an attribute of appointment, when the clinic starts recording a room's capacity and equipment.

workedSteps.text: Begin with room as a column. An appointment row holds a date, a start time and a room number, and while the clinic records nothing else about rooms the column is enough.
The clinic now wants each room's capacity and equipment, and those are facts with their own subject.
workedSteps.math: capacity, equipment: facts about a room

workedSteps.text: A room therefore has facts of its own and is told apart one by one, so it passes the test for an entity and gets a table.
The appointment keeps only the room's number as a pointer. A room hosts many appointments and an appointment takes place in one room, so the relationship is one-to-many.

steps.headline: Count the largest possible link table for a smaller clinic with 3 doctors and 12 patients.

workedSteps.text: A link table has one row for each patient-doctor pair that has met, and no pair appears twice.
One patient can pair with each of the 3 doctors, so that patient takes at most 3 rows.
With 12 patients, the most rows is the number of patients times the number of doctors. Work it out.

reveal.text: Member to Loan is one-to-many in the same way, and Member to Book is many-to-many, with Loan as the entity between them.

lessons.orientation: Read a short description of a business and list its entities, attributes and relationships with their cardinalities.
lessons.nextAction: Turn each relationship into foreign keys and junction tables, and query across them.

blocks.text: Here is how a clinic might describe itself: "The clinic has 4 doctors and 30 patients. Patients book appointments, each with one doctor, at a start time and in a numbered room, and the clinic keeps each patient's phone number." Every clause states a fact about the business, but a database stores tables and not sentences, so before any table can be created someone has to decide which clauses name a kind of thing, which give a fact about a thing, and which say how two kinds of thing are connected.

That decision is called **data modelling**, and it comes before the SQL you already know, because a join can only combine tables that exist and a query can only ask about columns that someone chose to store. A wrong decision here is expensive later, since a fact stored with the wrong thing gets repeated or lost and no query can repair that. Settling those questions from the description, before any table exists, tells you what the tables will hold and how they connect.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a description of a business and list its entities, attributes and relationships, with the cardinality of each relationship.
intro.whyItMatters: A model fixed before the tables exist is cheap to change; one found wrong with data in it is not.

recap.keyIdea: Entities are the kinds of thing a system must tell apart, attributes are single facts about one entity, and the cardinality of each relationship must be stated from both ends.

blocks.text: Reading the clinic description gave three entities, patient, doctor and appointment, with facts such as the date and start time attached to the appointment because that is what each one describes. The link between patient and doctor was many-to-many, so the appointment entity sits between them as the 'many' end of two one-to-many relationships.
A noun is an entity only when the system must identify individual ones and record facts about them, and a room that gains a capacity of its own is promoted from column to table.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns each relationship into columns and tables, using foreign keys and junction tables.

lessons.title: Foreign keys and junction tables

reveal.text: Each order belongs to exactly one customer, so the order rows are where a single value is enough.

steps.headline: A foreign key is a column whose values must match a key in another table, and in a one-to-many relationship it goes on the many side.

lead.text: Each order belongs to one customer, so the order row can hold that customer as a single value: the customer's id. A column that holds the id of a row in another table is called a **foreign key**, and the figure shows what it does. Order 103 has the number 2 in its customer_id column, and the customer with id 2 is Ben, so the number is all the database needs to find him. The customers table keeps one row per customer, and the orders table refers to it, never the other way round.

The rule that follows is that the foreign key goes on the **many side** of a one-to-many relationship. Many orders can point at the same customer, because several rows may store the same number, while a customer row could not point at several orders with a single value. In SQL the column is declared with the table it refers to: customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id).

afterFigure.text: The REFERENCES clause makes the database check the link as well as store it. An insert of an order with customer_id 9 is refused if no customer has the id 9, so an order cannot point at a customer that does not exist. PostgreSQL and SQLite both support this, although SQLite checks foreign keys only after you switch them on with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.

diagram.alt: Two tables, customers and orders. Each order row stores a customer_id, and an arrow runs from the order row to the customer row with that id.

reveal.text: Reading a schema this way, by asking which column holds another table's id, finds every relationship in it.

steps.headline: A many-to-many relationship is stored as a table of pairs, one row for each pair, never as a list of ids in a column.

lead.text: Students and courses are many-to-many: Ana takes Databases and Algorithms, and Databases has Ana, Ben and Chloe. Neither table can hold a single foreign key, since each student has several courses and each course several students. The tempting fix is a list of ids in one column, "10,11" in Ana's row. The database treats that as one piece of text, so it cannot check that 10 and 11 are real courses, it cannot build an index on the ids inside it, and a join has nothing to match.

The solution is a third table with one row for each student-course pair, called a **junction table**. It holds two foreign keys, one to each side, so every cell contains a single value and the one many-to-many relationship becomes two one-to-many relationships, which is the same step as the appointment table in the clinic. For seven pairs the junction table has seven rows.

afterFigure.text: Look at the two views for course 11. In the list view the answer has to be found by reading inside text, while in the junction table it is the two rows whose course_id is 11.

reveal.text: The count is a count of rows, which is what a junction table makes possible.

steps.headline: The pair of foreign keys identifies a junction row, and a fact about the pair, such as a grade, is a column of the junction table.

lead.text: A junction table needs a rule that stops the same pair being stored twice. If (1,10) could appear two times, Ana would seem to be enrolled twice on Databases, and counting rows would give wrong answers. The rule is that the combination of the two foreign keys is the **key of the junction table**: the pair (student_id, course_id) must be different in every row, and the database refuses a duplicate. In SQL this is written PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id).

The junction table also gives a home to a fact about the pair. Ana's grade in Databases describes neither Ana, who has a grade in every course she takes, nor Databases, which has a grade for every student, so it describes the combination. A fact of this kind is an [[attribute|One fact about one entity, stored as a column. Met in 'From a story to entities'.]] of the relationship, and it becomes a column of the junction table: enrollments(student_id, course_id, grade).

reveal.text: A column in the junction table has exactly one value for each pair, which a grade needs.

steps.headline: Reading back through a junction table takes a join on each side of it, and the result has one row for each pair.

lead.text: To list who takes what, a query follows the relationships in reverse. It starts at students, joins enrollments on student_id, and then joins courses on course_id, so the junction table is a stepping stone between the two entities. Without any filter the result has one row for every row of enrollments, which here is seven. Add the condition WHERE c.title = 'Databases' and only the pairs that mention that course remain, so the three students on it appear.

The figure shows the second hop on its own, joining enrollments to courses. Choose each query and compare the result with the two tables: every row of the first result comes from a single row of enrollments, with the course's title looked up through the key, and the second query counts those rows for each title, giving 3 for Databases and 2 each for Algorithms and Compilers. This is the join you wrote in SQL: From Rows to Reports, and the model decides which join paths exist.

queries.label: Course titles for each enrolment
queries.sql: SELECT e.student_id, c.title FROM enrollments e JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = e.course_id ORDER BY e.student_id, c.title;

queries.label: Students on each course
queries.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(*) AS students FROM enrollments e JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = e.course_id GROUP BY c.title ORDER BY c.title;

steps.headline: List the students enrolled in both Databases and Algorithms.

workedSteps.text: Join students to enrollments to courses, so that each of the seven pairs carries a name and a title.
Keep only the pairs whose title is Databases or Algorithms, using WHERE c.title IN ('Databases', 'Algorithms').
Group the remaining rows by student and count the distinct titles in each group. Ana has Databases and Algorithms, Ben has Databases only, and Chloe has both once the Compilers row is gone.
A student on both courses has exactly two distinct titles, so HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.title) = 2 keeps the groups for Ana and Chloe.

steps.headline: Change the query to ask for Databases and Compilers, and follow the same steps.

workedSteps.text: The filter keeps the pairs whose title is Databases or Compilers: (1,10), (2,10), (3,10), (3,12) and (4,12).
Grouping by student gives one distinct title for Ana, Ben and Dev, and two for Chloe.
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.title) = 2 keeps only the groups with two titles. Count the students that remain.

reveal.text: The junction table is recipe_ingredients(recipe_id, ingredient_id, amount), with the two ids together as its key, exactly as enrollments holds the grade.

lessons.orientation: Implement one-to-many relationships with foreign keys and many-to-many relationships with junction tables, and query across them.
lessons.nextAction: Choose keys for each table and add constraints that make the database refuse bad rows.

blocks.text: In a table of orders, orders 101 and 102 belong to Ana and order 103 belongs to Ben, and the table records this with a single number in each row, the id of the customer, which is 1 for Ana and 2 for Ben. Nothing else connects an order to a customer, and the database finds Ana by looking for the row of the customers table whose id is 1.

That one number is how every relationship from the last lesson is stored, because a row that holds another row's id can be followed to it, and the database can check that the id belongs to a row that exists. Placed in the table on the many side it stores a one-to-many relationship, and a table whose rows are pairs of such numbers stores a many-to-many one. With that device you can decide where the link between any two entities belongs and write the join that reads it back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a foreign key on the right side, build a junction table for a many-to-many relationship, and join across it.
intro.whyItMatters: A relationship that is stored as ordinary columns can be checked and queried by the database.

recap.keyIdea: A one-to-many relationship is stored as a foreign key on the many side, and a many-to-many relationship is stored as a junction table of pairs.

blocks.text: Order 103 held the number 2, and that single value was enough to find Ben, which is why the foreign key sits where each row has exactly one partner. A junction table does the same for students and courses, with one row per pair, the pair as its key, and any fact about the pair, such as a grade, as a column.
Queries then read back through the junction with two joins, and a condition on how many distinct courses each student has finds those on both.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what makes a key a good key, and at the constraints that let the database refuse bad rows.

lessons.title: Keys and constraints

steps.headline: A primary key identifies each row, and a good one is unique, never null and does not change.

lead.text: Look at what happens to a key when the real world changes. The email identifies the customer's row, so every order that refers to the customer holds a copy of it, and the change must be made in the customers row and in each of those orders. The figure shows Ana's case: with the email as key, one new address means three rows to rewrite, and with a generated number as key it means one cell.

A **primary key** is a column, or a set of columns, whose value is different in every row and is never empty, so that it identifies the row exactly. The example shows what else a good key needs. It must be **stable**, because other tables store copies of it, and a value that can change in the real world, such as an address or a name, is a poor choice even when it happens to be unique today.

afterFigure.text: PostgreSQL and SQLite both enforce the first two properties for you: PRIMARY KEY refuses a duplicate and refuses NULL. Stability is the one property that the database cannot check, and so it is the one the designer has to choose.

reveal.text: The cost grows with every row that copies the key, which is the reason designers often avoid keys that come from the outside world.

steps.headline: A natural key comes from the data, and a surrogate key is a meaningless identifier generated by the database.

lead.text: A key taken from the data itself, such as an ISBN or a product code, is called a **natural key**. Its attraction is that it already means something, and its risk is the one just seen: anything meaningful can be renumbered, corrected or reused. A **surrogate key** is a number that the database generates and that means nothing outside it, so there is no reason for it ever to change. In PostgreSQL it is written id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, and in SQLite id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY fills it in.

A surrogate key does not make the natural value disappear. The product code is still a fact about the product that must be different for each product, and for that the table declares it UNIQUE, which the next screen describes. The id is what other tables refer to, and the code remains something users can search by and change in one place.

reveal.text: The natural value usually stays in the table as a UNIQUE column, so users can still search by it.

steps.headline: A constraint makes the database refuse data that breaks a rule, whichever program sends it.

lead.text: A rule kept only in an application is a rule kept only for that application, since a script, a second program or a bug can all write to the table without going through it. A **constraint** is a rule declared on the table, and the database checks it for every writer. NOT NULL refuses an empty value. UNIQUE refuses a value that another row already has. CHECK refuses a row for which a condition is false, such as price >= 0. In the figure the three statements meet these rules in turn, and the one that breaks none is accepted.

UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY are related and not the same. A table has *one* primary key, which is unique and never null, but it can have many UNIQUE columns, and a UNIQUE column that allows NULL may hold several of them, because NULL means "unknown" and two unknowns are not known to be equal. The statement that is refused leaves the table as it was, so the rows already there are untouched.

steps.headline: A foreign key refuses a row with no parent, and a delete action says what happens to child rows when a parent is deleted.

lead.text: A foreign key is a constraint as well. An insert of an enrollment for student 9 is refused if no student has the id 9, so no row can refer to something that does not exist. The same rule applies when a parent row is removed while children still point to it, and there the designer chooses the outcome. NO ACTION, which is the default, and RESTRICT refuse the delete. ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the children too. ON DELETE SET NULL keeps them and clears the reference, which needs a column that allows NULL.

The figure deletes Ana, who has two of the three orders. Under no action nothing changes, under cascade her two orders go with her and one remains, and under set null all three orders stay and two lose their customer. Which one is right depends on whether an order means anything without its customer. SQLite checks foreign keys only after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.

reveal.text: A cascade is convenient and dangerous in equal measure, since one delete can remove many rows in other tables.

steps.headline: Check three statements against enrollments, which has key (student_id, course_id) and a foreign key to students.

workedSteps.text: INSERT (1,10,90) uses a pair that is already in the table, so the key rule fails.
INSERT (9,10,80) has a new pair, but student 9 does not exist.
DELETE student 3 with the default NO ACTION is refused, because three enrollments rows still refer to the student. With ON DELETE CASCADE it succeeds and removes those three rows.

steps.headline: Walk five statements against products (id key, code UNIQUE NOT NULL, price CHECK >= 0), starting from two rows.

workedSteps.text: Statement 1 has a new id, a new code and a valid price, so it passes every rule and is stored.
Statements 2 to 5 break the key, UNIQUE, CHECK and NOT NULL rules in turn, and each is refused whole.
A refused statement leaves nothing behind. Count the rows the table holds at the end.

reveal.text: If phone had to be present for every member it would also be declared NOT NULL, and then no two members could leave it empty.

lessons.orientation: Choose primary keys, and predict which statements a table's constraints accept or refuse.
lessons.nextAction: Find the anomalies in a wide table, and write the functional dependencies that explain them.

blocks.text: A key is the column, or the group of columns, that identifies a row, and its value has to be different in every row. A customers table could use the email address for this, since no two customers share one, and every order would then store that address to say whose order it is. The choice stops working when Ana changes her address, because the address belongs to her and she can change it whenever she likes, and every order that copied the old one now holds an address that no customer has.

Choosing a key that stays the same is half of making a table dependable, and the other half is deciding what the table will refuse. A rule such as "a price is never negative" written into one program holds only for that program, while the same rule declared on the table holds for every script, import and application that writes to it. Settling both tells you, for any statement sent to a table, whether it will be stored or turned away.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose a primary key, and to predict which statements a table's constraints will accept or refuse.
intro.whyItMatters: A rule declared on the table holds for every program, while a rule in application code holds only for that program.

recap.keyIdea: A good primary key is unique, never null and stable, and constraints make the database refuse any row that breaks a declared rule.

blocks.text: A surrogate key is the usual choice because it carries no meaning that can change, while the natural value stays in the table as a UNIQUE column. NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and foreign keys then refuse bad rows whichever program sends them, and a delete action decides what happens to child rows.
A refused statement changes nothing, so predicting a table's contents after a run of statements means checking each one against the rules in turn.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows what goes wrong when a table is wider than the facts it holds, and gives the vocabulary to explain it.

lessons.title: Anomalies and functional dependencies

reveal.text: Three rows had to change, although there is only one fact to change.

steps.headline: Repeating a fact in many rows invites an update anomaly, where one copy is changed and the others are left behind.

lead.text: The table orders_flat holds customers, products and orders in one place, and so it repeats facts. Ana's email is stored on each of her three rows, and the price of a Pen on each row that mentions a Pen. Storing the same fact more than once is called **redundancy**. People often take its cost to be disk space, which for four rows is nothing, but the real cost is that the copies can *disagree*.

If Ana's address is changed in two rows and missed in the third, the table now says two different things about her, and no query can tell which is right. An error that the structure of a table makes possible in this way is called an **anomaly**, and this one, where a fact is changed in some copies and not others, is an **update anomaly**. The figure lets you pull out the rows for Ana and for Pen: three rows repeat Ana's email and two repeat the price of a Pen, which is why a price change to 3 has to touch two rows.

queries.label: Ana's rows
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders_flat WHERE customer_name = 'Ana' ORDER BY order_id, product;

queries.label: Rows for Pen
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders_flat WHERE product = 'Pen' ORDER BY order_id;

reveal.text: Every extra copy is a place where an update can be missed.

steps.headline: The same table also loses facts when a row is deleted and has nowhere to keep a fact that has no order yet.

lead.text: Order 2 is Ben's only order, so the row for order 2 is the only place his name and email are stored. If the order is deleted, perhaps because it was cancelled, Ben is deleted with it, and the table no longer knows that he was a customer. Losing a fact that was only ever stored beside another is a **delete anomaly**.

The opposite problem is an **insert anomaly**. The shop begins to stock a Cap at price 3, and no one has ordered one. The price is a fact about the product, but a row of this table is an order line, which needs an order_id and a qty, and the table has no row that could hold a Cap alone without inventing them. Both problems come from the same cause, since one table stores facts about three different kinds of thing.

reveal.text: The three kinds, update, delete and insert, all trace back to facts about different things sharing one table.

steps.headline: A functional dependency X → Y holds when rows that agree on X always agree on Y, and the business rule decides which ones hold.

lead.text: The vocabulary for what went wrong is a **functional dependency**. We write X → Y, and say that X *determines* Y, when any two rows with the same value of X always have the same value of Y. Each order has one customer, so order_id → customer_email: the two rows of order 1 both say ana@x.io. Each email belongs to one customer, so customer_email → customer_name, and each product has one price, so product → product_price. Quantity is different, because it needs two columns: order 1 bought 10 Pens and 2 Inks, so neither order_id nor product alone fixes it, but the pair (order_id, product) → qty.

A dependency comes from the *meaning* of the business and is not something read off the sample. In these four rows product_price → product also holds, because the prices 2, 5 and 4 happen to be different, but the shop may price two products the same, and then it would fail. The rows can show that a dependency is false, since a counterexample refutes it, and they can never prove one true.

steps.headline: A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that determines every other column, and a table can have more than one.

lead.text: A dependency answers the question of what identifies a row. A **candidate key** is a set of columns that determines every column of the table and that has no unnecessary members: remove any column and it stops determining everything. In orders_flat, order_id alone fixes the customer and the email but not the product, since order 1 has two products. Product alone fixes only the price. The pair (order_id, product) fixes the customer through the order, the price through the product, and the quantity through both, so it is a candidate key.

Designers sometimes speak as if a table has one key and the rest is extra, but a table may have several candidate keys. A users table with an id, an email and a username, each different in every row, has three, and the designer picks one as the primary key. The unchosen ones are usually kept as UNIQUE columns.

steps.headline: Find a candidate key of orders_flat from its dependencies.

workedSteps.text: Start with order_id. It determines customer_email, and customer_email determines customer_name, so it reaches three columns.
It cannot be a key alone, because the product, price and quantity are still not fixed. Order 1 has two rows with different products.
Add product. It determines product_price, and the pair determines qty, so all six columns are now reached.
Drop either column and some column is lost, since order_id without product loses the price and product without order_id loses the customer, so the pair is minimal.

reveal.text: The shape is the same as orders_flat: two columns that each fix some facts, and a pair that fixes the fact about both.

lessons.orientation: Find update, insert and delete anomalies in a wide table, and write the functional dependencies that explain them.
lessons.nextAction: Split the wide table into second and third normal form, and check that nothing is lost.

blocks.text: The table orders_flat keeps everything about a shop's sales in one place. For each product on each order it records the customer's name and email, the product with its price, and the quantity, so a single row answers the question of who bought what. The convenience has a price, because a customer's email is written again for every line she has ordered, and a product's price is written again for every order that includes it.

A fact written in several places can later be changed in some of them and not in others, and then the table says two different things about the same customer, with nothing in it to show which is right. The cause is always a rule of the business that the table does not respect, such as that each order has exactly one customer, and stating those rules is how you predict where a wide table will go wrong and find the columns that identify a row.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find update, insert and delete anomalies in a wide table, write the functional dependencies behind them, and find a candidate key.
intro.whyItMatters: Anomalies are the practical reason to split tables, and dependencies are the tool that says where to split.

recap.keyIdea: A table that repeats facts invites update, insert and delete anomalies, and functional dependencies say which facts belong together and which columns form a candidate key.

blocks.text: The four rows of orders_flat showed all three anomalies: Ana's email had to change in three places, deleting order 2 erased Ben, and a new product had no row to live in. Each problem traces to a dependency such as order_id → customer_email that the table does not respect.
A candidate key is the smallest set of columns that determines everything, here (order_id, product), and the dependencies that start from only part of it are the ones to remove.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these dependencies to decompose the table into normal forms.

lessons.title: Normal forms and lossless decomposition

reveal.text: The join returned more rows than the table had, which a correct decomposition never does.

steps.headline: A split that does not follow a dependency can invent rows when the pieces are joined, so the split is not lossless.

lead.text: Joining ep and ps on project gives four rows: the two original ones, (Ana, P1, SQL) and (Ben, P1, Rust), and two that were never in the table, (Ana, P1, Rust) and (Ben, P1, SQL). The extra rows are **spurious rows**. They appear because project is not a key of either piece, since P1 occurs twice in both, so each side matches *several* rows on the other. The split has thrown information away, namely which employee used which skill, and no join can recover it.

A decomposition is **lossless** when joining the pieces returns exactly the original rows, and a decomposition that is not lossless is *lossy*. The guarantee is that the columns the pieces share are a key of at least one piece, because then each row on the other side matches exactly one row there and no multiplication can happen. Every split in this lesson will be checked against that test.

queries.label: Join on project
queries.sql: SELECT ep.employee, ep.project, ps.skill FROM ep JOIN ps ON ps.project = ep.project ORDER BY ep.employee, ps.skill;

queries.label: Count the joined rows
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM ep JOIN ps ON ps.project = ep.project;

reveal.text: The two rows that were invented look as valid as the real ones, which is why a lossy split cannot be detected from the pieces alone.

steps.headline: First normal form requires one value in each cell, so a column holding a list has to become rows.

lead.text: The first of the normal forms is the simplest to state. A table is in **first normal form** when every cell holds a single value. A column called phone1, phone2, a list such as "555-0101, 555-0188" in one cell, or a nested row all break it, for the reason met in the last lesson: the database cannot check, index or join on a value that is really several. The remedy is the one used for a many-to-many relationship, which is a row for each value, normally in a table of its own.

The word *normal* comes from relational theory. E. F. Codd's 1970 paper already described replacing relations that contain nested relations with simple ones, and the stricter forms that follow are all conditions of this kind on the dependencies in a table. Each form adds a condition to the one before, so a table in third normal form is also in second and first.

steps.headline: Second normal form removes every dependency on part of a key by moving the partly dependent columns to a table of their own.

lead.text: A table is in **second normal form** when it is in first and no non-key column depends on *part* of a candidate key. The check starts from the key found in the last lesson. In orders_flat the key is (order_id, product), but the customer columns depend on order_id alone and product_price depends on product alone, so both are partial dependencies. Only qty needs the whole pair.

The remedy is to move each partly dependent group out to a table whose key is the part it depends on. The figure shows the result: orders(order_id, customer_email, customer_name), products(product, product_price) and order_items(order_id, product, qty). Every non-key column now depends on the whole key of its own table.

afterFigure.text: A table whose key is a single column cannot have a partial dependency, since there is no smaller part, which is why second normal form only ever matters for composite keys.

reveal.text: Third normal form deals with a different pattern: a non-key column depending on another non-key column.

steps.headline: Third normal form removes dependencies of one non-key column on another, which moves customers out of orders.

lead.text: Look at orders(order_id, customer_email, customer_name) after the second step. Its key is order_id, and customer_email depends on it, which is fine, but customer_name depends on customer_email and only reaches the key through it. A non-key column that depends on another non-key column is a **transitive dependency**, and a table with none, in addition to being in second normal form, is in **third normal form**. The remedy is the same as before: the dependent column goes to a table keyed by what it depends on.

That gives customers its own table, and with generated ids the schema in the figure has four tables. customers has 2 rows, products 3, orders 3 and order_items 4. Ana's name is now stored in 1 cell instead of 3, so an address change touches one row, deleting an order cannot delete a customer, and a new product can be inserted before anyone orders it.

afterFigure.text: The two forms are easy to mix up. The second concerns a column depending on *part of a key*; the third concerns a non-key column depending on *another non-key column*.

lessons.orientation: Decompose a table into second and third normal form and check that joining the pieces gives back exactly the original rows.
lessons.nextAction: Describe a star schema, and decide when to duplicate data on purpose.

blocks.text: Take a table of two rows, (Ana, P1, SQL) and (Ben, P1, Rust), which record that Ana used SQL on project P1 and that Ben used Rust on the same project. Cut it in two by columns, one piece holding employee and project and the other holding project and skill, and every value is still stored in one piece or the other. Joining the pieces on project is the obvious way to put the table back together.

Whether the join restores the original depends on how the columns are tied to one another, which the last lesson showed how to write down as dependencies. A split that follows the dependencies is safe, and the standard way to find one for a wide table is to apply the normal forms in turn, checking each result by joining the pieces and comparing the rows with the original. That makes it possible to repair a table like the one in the last lesson and to show that nothing was lost in doing so.

recap.keyIdea: Normalising splits a table along its dependencies, up to third normal form, so that each fact is stored once, and the split is lossless when the shared columns are a key of one piece.

blocks.text: The flat orders table became customers, orders, products and order_items by removing partial dependencies for second normal form and then the dependency of customer_name on customer_email for third. Joining the four tables returned the same four rows, with Ana's revenue still 34 and Ben's 8, while the badly cut table returned four rows from two.
Normalising stops once every fact is stored once, and it has a cost: reading the data back takes joins.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at reporting, where the cost of those joins is sometimes worth avoiding.

lessons.title: Reporting models and denormalisation

steps.headline: A fact table records one row for each event, with numbers and keys, and leaves the descriptions to other tables.

lead.text: A database does two quite different jobs. One is recording changes safely, as an order is placed or an item added, which is the work the earlier lessons designed for: every fact stored once. The other is answering a question over many rows, such as the revenue for each month and product category, which reads a great deal and changes little. The figure shows the six sales of a small shop. Each row is one sale, and every column is either a number to add up or a key pointing at something that describes it.

A table of this kind is a **fact table**: it has one row for each event, a few numeric **measures** such as units and amount, and foreign keys to the tables that say who, what and when. It is usually the largest table in a reporting database, which is why it holds as little text as possible.

reveal.text: The cost grows with the number of fact rows that carry the copy, and a fact table is usually the largest table in the database.

steps.headline: A star schema puts a fact table at the centre and joins it to small dimension tables that hold the descriptions.

lead.text: The tables that describe the facts are called **dimensions**. Here dim_product holds a name and a category for each product, and dim_date holds the day and month for each date. A dimension is small next to the fact table, because a shop has few products and a year has 365 days, and it is wide, with many descriptive columns, because those are the things a report groups by. Drawn with the fact table in the middle and one line to each dimension, the layout looks like a star, and so it is called a **star schema**.

The key point is where each kind of information lives. The numbers to be added, units and amount, belong to the event and stay in the fact table. The words to group by, category and month, belong to the thing described and stay in a dimension, once. The second view of the figure shows the report that these tables produce.

steps.headline: A report joins the fact table to the dimensions it needs and groups by their columns, adding up a measure.

lead.text: Revenue by month and category takes three tables. The query joins fact_sales to dim_date on date_id and to dim_product on product_id, groups the rows by month and category, and adds up amount in each group: SELECT d.month, p.category, SUM(f.amount) FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_id = f.date_id JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_id = f.product_id GROUP BY d.month, p.category. This is the join and GROUP BY of *SQL: From Rows to Reports*, and the star layout means every report needs the same shape of query, with a different choice of dimension columns.

The figure here joins one dimension at a time. Grouped by category the 84 of revenue splits into 24 for Kitchen and 60 for Stationery, and grouped by product name it splits into 8, 60 and 16. Nothing in the fact table changed between the two reports, and only the dimension column in GROUP BY changed.

queries.label: Revenue by category
queries.sql: SELECT p.category, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_id = f.product_id GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY p.category;

queries.label: Revenue by product
queries.sql: SELECT p.name, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_id = f.product_id GROUP BY p.name ORDER BY p.name;

reveal.text: The report is four such cells, one for each month and category present in the facts.

steps.headline: Denormalising stores a copy of a fact on purpose to avoid a join, and the copy needs a rule that keeps it in step.

lead.text: Reporting schemas break the rule of the previous lessons on purpose, since the category is repeated for every product and a month for every day. Denormalisation can also be used inside an ordinary database. An orders table might store a column total, a copy of the sum of its items' prices, so that showing an order's total no longer means reading and adding every item. The price is that the copy must be updated whenever an item is added, changed or removed, through a trigger or through application code, and a missed update is the update anomaly again.

So denormalisation is a decision, and it comes *after* normalising and measuring, not before. It is worth making when reads far outnumber changes to the source, when the computation is slow enough to matter, when the copy is cheap to keep in step, and when a drift between copy and source could be detected and repaired. A reporting schema does the same on a larger scale, and works because its facts are written once and then rarely changed.

afterFigure.text: In the 1990s Ralph Kimball popularised the dimensional design shown here, with measures in a central fact table and descriptions around it.

reveal.text: It is a deliberate step taken after measuring, and never the first design.

steps.headline: Decide whether to store a copy of an order's total, given 1000 reads and 20 item changes a day.

workedSteps.text: Normalise first. The total is computable as the sum of the item amounts, so the design has no copy yet.
Measure the read and write counts. The shop reads totals 1000 times a day and changes an item 20 times.
The copy costs one extra update for each item change, so 20 extra updates a day, in return for removing the sum from 1000 reads.
A trigger can keep the copy in step, and a nightly query comparing each total with its sum can detect any drift. With both in place the copy is worth keeping.
workedSteps.math: copy it, with a trigger and a check

steps.headline: Judge the same copy for a shop with 600 reads and 300 item changes a day.

workedSteps.text: The total is again the sum of the item amounts, with no copy so far.
Each item change costs one update of the copy, and each read saves the sum.
Work out how many reads there are for each change.

reveal.text: The change is one row in a dimension, and every report that groups by category then reflects it.

lessons.orientation: Describe a star schema, and decide when to duplicate data on purpose.
lessons.nextAction: Estimate how many pages a table scan and an index lookup read.

blocks.text: When a shop records a sale, it writes one small row: which product was sold, on which day, how many units and for what amount, with the product and the day given only as keys into other tables. At the end of the month the manager asks for revenue by month and by product category, which means reading every sale and adding up the amounts in groups.

The first job is served by the design of the earlier lessons, in which every fact is stored once and a change touches one row. The second needs a different arrangement, because a report on the same tables must join several of them to reach the category and the month. Reports are usually built on a shape that keeps the numbers together in one table and the descriptions to group by in small tables around it, and an ordinary database sometimes copies a value on purpose for the same reason. In both cases something is traded, which is less joining for a fact that is now stored more than once and has to be kept right.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a star schema, write the joins for a report over its dimensions, and judge when copying data is worth its cost.
intro.whyItMatters: Repeating data is sometimes the right design, as long as the decision follows a measurement and the copy has a rule that keeps it right.

recap.keyIdea: A star schema keeps measures in a central fact table and descriptions in dimensions, and a deliberate copy of data is worth making only when measured reads outweigh the cost of keeping it in step.

blocks.text: The six sales gave 84 of revenue, which a report split by month and category into 16, 30, 8 and 30 with two joins from the fact table. A change of category touched one dimension row where a copy in the fact table would have touched two or three.
Denormalising reverses that discipline in one place, on purpose, and it needs a trigger or a rule to keep the copy right.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to speed, and asks how many pages a table scan and an index lookup must read.

lessons.title: How an index finds rows

steps.headline: A database reads and writes whole pages, so cost is counted in pages, and a scan reads every page of the table.

lead.text: A table with 1,000,000 rows is not read row by row. The database stores rows in fixed-size blocks called **pages**, 8 kB each in PostgreSQL, and always transfers a whole page at a time, so the useful measure of work is the number of pages read. With 50 rows on a page, 1,000,000 rows fill 1,000,000 ÷ 50 = 20,000 pages.

Without any help, finding one row means reading page after page until it turns up, and since the database cannot know in advance that a row is unique it must read them all. This is a **table scan**, and it costs 20,000 page reads however few rows match. The figure draws the 20,000 pages as 50 squares of 400 pages each. A scan colours all of them.

reveal.text: The cost depends only on the size of the table, which is why scans get slower as a table grows.
Each level multiplies the reach by the same number, which is what makes a tree so shallow.

steps.headline: A B-tree keeps keys in sorted pages that each lead to many children, so a few levels reach any row.

lead.text: An index is a structure kept beside the table to avoid the scan. The usual one is a **B-tree**, which is *not* a second sorted copy of the table. Its pages hold keys, in order, with a pointer beside each key: in the upper levels the pointer leads to a page one level down, and in the bottom level, the leaf pages, it gives the location of a row in the table. The number of children each page can have is its **fan-out**. A key is only a few bytes, so a page holds hundreds of them, and the examples here assume a fan-out of 100 to keep the arithmetic easy.

A lookup starts at the root page, reads which child covers the key it wants, moves to that page, and repeats until it reaches a leaf. The number of levels is the **height**, and it is the smallest h for which 100^h is at least the number of rows. For 1,000,000 rows, 100^3 = 1,000,000, so the height is 3. The figure follows one lookup, counting a page read at every step.

afterFigure.text: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight described B-trees in 1970 while working at Boeing, and the structure is still the default index in PostgreSQL and SQLite.

diagram.alt: A B-tree with a root page, a layer of middle pages, a layer of leaf pages and the table pages beneath. Five views follow one lookup downward, counting the pages read: none, then the root, middle, leaf and finally the table page, four reads in all.

reveal.text: A hundred times as many rows added only one level, which is why index lookups scale so well.

steps.headline: A lookup reads one page for each level plus the table page that holds the row, which is a tiny fraction of a scan.

lead.text: The cost of finding one row by index is therefore the height of the tree plus one read of the table page that the leaf points to. For the table of 1,000,000 rows that is 3 + 1 = 4 page reads, against 20,000 for the scan, which is 20,000 ÷ 4 = 5,000 times fewer.

The tree stays shallow however large the table grows. With a fan-out of 100, a billion rows need only 5 levels, because 100^4 = 100,000,000 is too few and 100^5 = 10,000,000,000 is enough. Real fan-outs are often several hundred, so real trees are no taller. The price is paid on writes, since every insert or delete must also update the index pages, which is why a table is not given an index on every column.

steps.headline: Compare a scan with an index lookup for a table of 100,000,000 rows, 50 rows on a page, fan-out 100.

workedSteps.text: The table occupies 100,000,000 ÷ 50 pages, and a scan reads all of them.
The B-tree needs the smallest h with 100^h at least 100,000,000.
A lookup reads one page for each level and one table page for the row.
The ratio is the scan cost divided by the lookup cost.

steps.headline: Repeat the comparison for 10,000,000 rows at 50 rows per page.

workedSteps.text: The table occupies 10,000,000 ÷ 50 = 200,000 pages, all of which a scan reads.
The tree has 4 levels, so a lookup reads 4 index pages and 1 table page, which is 5 reads.
Divide the scan cost by the lookup cost.

steps.headline: An index lookup wins when few rows match, and a scan wins when so many match that reading the table in order is cheaper.

lead.text: A lookup of a single row costs 4 reads, but a query that matches many rows must follow the index to each one, and those table pages are scattered. Reading scattered pages is slower than reading neighbouring ones, because the disk cannot read ahead. Take the simple model in which each row found through the index costs 4 sequential page reads' worth of time, while a scan costs 20,000 sequential reads. The two are equal when the number of matching rows times 4 equals 20,000, which is 5,000 rows, or 0.5 percent of a table of 1,000,000.

Beyond that point the scan is cheaper, even though the index exists. This is why a database planner sometimes ignores an index, and why an index does not always help: it serves queries that match a small share of the rows. The figure shows the cost of each as the number of matching rows grows.

afterFigure.text: PostgreSQL makes the same comparison with its own cost settings, and a later lesson shows where the planner's choice appears in a query plan.

diagram.alt: A line chart of cost in page reads against the number of matching rows. The scan is a flat line at 20,000. The index line rises by 4 for each row. The lines cross at 5,000 rows. Three views mark 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 matching rows.

An index helps most with selective queries, and the next lesson shows how to measure and increase that selectivity.

lessons.orientation: Estimate the pages read by a table scan and an index lookup from page size and fan-out.
lessons.nextAction: Decide which queries an index on two columns can serve, and estimate how many rows a filter matches.

blocks.text: A table of 1,000,000 rows with 50 rows on each page occupies 20,000 pages, and a database reads whole pages and never single rows. To find one customer in such a table without any other structure, it has to read page after page until the row turns up, and since it cannot know that no second matching row exists, it reads all 20,000 of them.

With an index on the column being searched, the same customer is found in four page reads, because the index leads from the value to the row through a few levels of index pages and not through the table. The four comes from arithmetic on rows, pages and the number of entries a page can hold, and the same arithmetic shows the point at which an index stops being faster than reading everything.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate the pages read by a table scan and by an index lookup, and say when the index stops helping.
intro.whyItMatters: Estimating in pages tells you whether a query will take a moment or a minute before you run it.

recap.keyIdea: A B-tree finds a row in height plus one page reads, so a lookup costs a handful of pages where a scan costs the whole table, until a query matches enough rows that the scan wins.

blocks.text: Pages, not rows, are the unit of cost: 1,000,000 rows at 50 per page are 20,000 pages, while a B-tree of fan-out 100 reaches any of them in 3 index pages and 1 table page. The ratio of 5,000 grows with the table, since a hundredfold increase in rows adds only one level.
An index path costs more for each matching row, and under the simple model used here it matches the scan at about 0.5 percent of the table, so broad queries are better served without it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at indexes on two columns, and at how selective a filter must be for an index to pay.

lessons.title: Composite indexes and selectivity

reveal.text: Entries for one first name are spread across the list, because the order was decided by last name first.

steps.headline: An index on two columns is sorted by the first and then by the second, so it can seek on the first column, or on both, and never on the second alone.

lead.text: An index on (last_name, first_name) is a [[B-tree|A sorted tree of pages that leads to a row in a few reads. Met in 'How an index finds rows'.]] whose keys are the pair, sorted by last_name and then, among equal last names, by first_name. That is the order of a phone book. All the Smiths are next to each other, so the search finds the first one and reads along until the name changes. The Anas are not next to each other, because first names are in order only *within* a last name.

The consequence is the **leftmost-prefix rule**. The index can seek on the first column, on the first two together, and on a range of the first column, since a range of last names is a contiguous run. It cannot seek on first_name alone, because no single place in the index holds all the Anas. The figure sorts the filters into those that seek and those that do not, and the order of the columns in the index is therefore a design decision, and not a detail.

afterFigure.text: Two separate indexes, one on each column, are not the same as one composite index. The database can sometimes combine them, but at a higher cost than one seek.

diagram.alt: Predicates against an index on last name and first name. One view lists four that can seek: equality on last name, equality on both, a range on last name, and equality on last name with a range on first name. The other lists two that cannot: first name alone, and a pattern with a leading wildcard.

reveal.text: A filter on the second column alone has no starting point in the index.

steps.headline: Selectivity is the share of rows a condition keeps, and an index pays off only when that share is small.

lead.text: Whether an index is worth having depends on how many rows each value leads to. A country column with 250 values spread evenly over 1,000,000 rows keeps about 1,000,000 ÷ 250 = 4,000 rows for each value, which is 0.4 percent of the table, below the break-even of the last lesson, so an index on it helps. The share of rows a condition keeps is its **selectivity**, and a small share is called *high* selectivity.

A status column with three values behaves differently. If 90 percent of the rows are 'done', the condition status = 'done' keeps 9 rows in 10, and an index on it saves almost nothing, since a scan would be cheaper. The same index can still be useful for the rare value: if 'failed' covers 1 percent of rows, status = 'failed' keeps 10,000 of them. Selectivity depends on the value asked for, as well as on the column.

reveal.text: Real columns are rarely even, so a planner keeps statistics about the common values, which a later lesson shows.

steps.headline: SQLite prints the access method for each table, and COVERING INDEX means the query never visits the table.

lead.text: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN prints one line for each table in a query, saying how it will be read. SCAN means every row, as when first_name alone is the filter. SEARCH ... USING INDEX means a seek in the index, and the part in brackets, such as (last_name=?), names the columns the seek used. SEARCH ... USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?) is the same for a lookup by id.

When an index holds *every* column a query reads, the table need not be visited at all. The query SELECT first_name FROM emp WHERE last_name = 'L3' needs only last_name and first_name, both in idx_name, so the plan says USING COVERING INDEX, and the lookup costs the tree height without the extra table page. An index like this is a **covering index** for that query. The figure shows the three lines with the query for each.

reveal.text: The plan line is the quickest way to check whether an index is being used.

steps.headline: Put equality columns first and a range column last, and an index can also hand back rows already in order.

lead.text: Take the query WHERE dept = 'D2' AND salary >= 50000. An index on (dept, salary) seeks to the start of the D2 block, and within that block the salaries are in order, so it seeks again to 50000 and reads to the end of the block. An index on (salary, dept) would have to read every salary from 50000 up across all departments, and discard the rows from other departments. The rule of thumb is that columns tested for *equality* come first and the column tested by a *range* comes last.

The same index serves an ORDER BY. Within one department the salaries are already sorted, so WHERE dept = 'D2' ORDER BY salary reads the rows in the order requested and needs no separate sort step. SQLite shows a sort as a plan line, USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY, and with this index that line is absent.

steps.headline: Choose between indexes on (dept, salary) and on (salary, dept) for WHERE dept = 'D2' AND salary >= 50000, on 12,000 employees in 4 departments.

workedSteps.text: The condition on dept is an equality, and the condition on salary is a range, so equality goes first.
With dept first, the seek lands in D2's block, which holds a quarter of the table.
Inside that block the salaries are sorted, so a second seek reaches 50000 and the rest of the block is read in order, without touching other departments.
With salary first, the matching rows are scattered between all four departments, and three quarters of the rows read from 50000 upward are discarded.

steps.headline: Estimate the rows matched by one country in a table of 2,000,000 rows.

workedSteps.text: The values are equally common, so each country gets an equal share of the table.
There are 250 countries and 2,000,000 rows.
Divide the rows by the number of values.

reveal.text: Here 60,000 rows is 6 percent of the table, well above the 0.5 percent break-even, so even this value would be read faster by a scan.

blocks.text: A phone book is sorted by last name and, among equal last names, by first name. Finding every Smith in it takes a moment, because the Smiths are printed together in one run, and an index on two columns, last name and then first name, is ordered in exactly this way.

Whether a query can use such an index depends on whether the rows it wants sit together in that order, and the question has a second half, which is how many rows a filter will keep, since an index that leads to half the table is not worth following. Answering both for a given query, and reading the line of a plan that shows what the database chose, settles which columns an index should have and in what order, before it is built.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which queries an index on two columns can serve, estimate the rows a filter matches, and read the access lines of a SQLite plan.
intro.whyItMatters: Most index problems are a wrong column order or a filter that keeps too many rows, and both can be seen before running a query.

recap.keyIdea: An index on (a, b) serves filters on a, or on a and b, and not on b alone, and it pays off only when the filter keeps a small share of the rows.

blocks.text: The leftmost-prefix rule follows from the order of the entries: sorted by the first column and then by the second within it, so a seek needs the first column. Equality columns go first and a range column last, and a covering index lets a query skip the table.
Selectivity decides whether the seek is worth it. A value that keeps 0.4 percent of the rows suits an index, while a status flag that keeps 90 percent does not.

lessons.title: Reading query plans

reveal.text: The direct method multiplies the two sizes, and the other strategies exist to avoid that product.

steps.headline: A nested loop checks pairs, a hash join builds a table and probes it, and a merge join walks two sorted inputs.

lead.text: There are three standard ways to join. A **nested loop** takes each row of the outer table and looks for matches in the inner one. If the inner table has no index on the join column it checks every row, so the work is the product of the two sizes, and if there *is* an index each lookup costs a seek, which for a three-level index is 3 index pages and 1 table page. A **hash join** reads one table into an in-memory hash table keyed on the join column, then reads the other table once and probes the hash table for each row, which is the two sizes added together. A **merge join** reads two inputs that are already sorted on the join column and walks along both together.

For R with 1,000 rows and S with 5,000 the figure shows 5,000,000 comparisons for the unindexed nested loop and 6,000 operations for the hash join. The indexed nested loop makes 1,000 seeks of 4 page reads, which is 4,000. The last number counts page reads and the others count row operations, so they say something about the order of magnitude only.

diagram.alt: Three ways of joining a table R of 1,000 rows with a table S of 5,000 rows: a nested loop with no index, a hash join, and a nested loop with an index on S. Each view shows the amount of work as a count.

steps.headline: A plan is a tree of steps with an estimated row count at each, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query to show the actual rows too.

lead.text: EXPLAIN shows the plan that PostgreSQL has chosen for a query without running it: a tree in which each node is one step, such as a scan, a join or a sort, with the planner's estimate of the rows it will produce. The tree is read from the *bottom*, since the scans at the leaves run first, their rows flow up into the join, and the join's rows flow up into the sort. EXPLAIN ANALYZE goes further, and actually *executes* the query, so it can add the real row count and time beside each estimate, but for that reason it must be used with care on a statement that changes data.

The first thing to look for in a plan is a step where the estimate and the actual count differ greatly. In the figure the scan of orders was estimated at 10 rows and returned 90,000. The join above it and the sort above that inherit the mistake, and the planner picked a strategy that suits 10 rows and not 90,000. Reading only the top line of a plan would have missed where it first went wrong.

diagram.alt: A query plan drawn as a tree. At the top is Sort, below it Hash Join, which has two inputs: Seq Scan on orders, and Hash over Seq Scan on customers. The first view shows each step's estimated rows. The second also shows the actual rows: the orders scan, the join and the sort were estimated at 10 rows and returned 90,000.

reveal.text: An error at a leaf is carried upward through every node that depends on it.

steps.headline: The planner estimates rows from stored statistics, so a large gap between estimate and actual usually means they are stale.

lead.text: The planner cannot count the rows a filter will keep without running it, so it estimates from **statistics** that the database keeps about each column: the number of rows, the most common values and how the rest are spread. When a table has changed a great deal since the statistics were gathered, or never had them gathered, the estimates drift, and the planner may choose a plan that would have suited the old data. The command ANALYZE refreshes them, and PostgreSQL's autovacuum normally runs it in the background.

Three misreadings are common. The planner does not always choose the same plan for the same query, because plans change with the size of the data and its statistics. A sequential scan in a plan is not always a mistake, since on a small table or a query that keeps most of the rows it is the cheapest method. And a plan is worth reading when a query is slow and you want to know *which step* to blame.

reveal.text: A ratio of that size usually leads the planner to the wrong join strategy.

steps.headline: Count the page reads of a nested-loop join of R, with 1,000 rows, to S, which has a 3-level index on the join column.

workedSteps.text: R is the outer table, so the loop runs once for each of its 1,000 rows.
Each iteration seeks in the index on S and then fetches the matching row.
The total is the number of iterations times the pages for one seek.
A hash join over the same tables does 1,000 + 5,000 = 6,000 operations, so the two are of the same order, and the planner picks by its cost estimates.

steps.headline: Repeat the count when the outer table has 2,000 rows.

workedSteps.text: The loop now runs 2,000 times, once for each row of R.
Each iteration reads 3 index pages and 1 table page.
Multiply the iterations by the pages for one seek.

reveal.text: A nested loop is the best choice when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index.
